{
  "measurements": [
    {
      "statistic": "face validity",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the degree to which animal models of voluntary drug intake and addiction resemble human behavior.",
      "compared": "animal models of addiction vs human behavior",
      "species": [
        "monkeys",
        "rats",
        "mice",
        "humans"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "The precondition for each animal model is a high degree of face validity, defined here as characteristic behavioral features that are seen both in laboratory animals and in humans."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "face validity",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the degree to which behavioral fear responses in mice and humans resemble each other.",
      "compared": "mouse freezing behavior vs human freezing behavior",
      "species": [
        "mice",
        "humans"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "For example, behavioral fear responses are critical to most species for survival and developed over millions of years. As such, freezing behavior in response to a threatening stimulus, as seen in mice and humans alike, has real face validity."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "face validity",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the degree to which drug self-administration behavior in mammals resembles drug intake behavior in humans from an evolutionary perspective.",
      "compared": "mammalian drug/alcohol intake behavior vs human drug/alcohol intake behavior",
      "species": [
        "mammals",
        "humans"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "These evolutionary roots of alcohol- and drug-taking behavior in mammals support the real face validity of animal models of drug self-administration."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "construct validity",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the assumption that the neurochemical and neuroanatomical substrates involved in drug-intake behavior are similar in laboratory rodents and humans.",
      "compared": "neurochemical and neuroanatomical substrates of drug intake in rodents vs humans",
      "species": [
        "rodents",
        "humans"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "As explained, these models have excellent face validity, and it is assumed that the neurochemical and neuroanatomical substrates involved in drug-intake behavior are similar in laboratory rodents and humans 8 , 9 (which is often defined as construct validity)."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "predictive validity",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the helpfulness of self-administration-based animal models in identifying strategies useful for intervening in human drug consumption.",
      "compared": "animal models of drug self-administration vs human drug consumption intervention strategies",
      "species": [
        "animals",
        "humans"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "Consequently, self-administration-based animal models are helpful in unraveling the molecular and neurobiological mechanisms of drug-related behaviors and therefore critical in identifying strategies useful in the intervention of human drug consumption; ie, they provide predictive validity."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "generalizability",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the extent to which preclinical data on opioid-receptor blockade reducing alcohol consumption in rats translates to the human situation where nalmefene also reduces alcohol consumption.",
      "compared": "opioid-receptor blockade reducing alcohol consumption in rats vs nalmefene reducing alcohol consumption in humans",
      "species": [
        "rats",
        "humans"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "For example, pharmacological opioid-receptor blockade reduces alcohol consumption in many self-administration studies in different strains of rats and mice under different conditions, 10 which provides generalizability of preclinical data that translates to the human situation, in which the opioid-receptor blocker nalmefene also reduces alcohol consumption. 11"
    },
    {
      "statistic": "face validity",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the degree to which the incubation of drug-seeking behavior in laboratory rats resembles the phenomenon in humans.",
      "compared": "incubation of drug-seeking in rats vs humans",
      "species": [
        "rats",
        "humans"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "It is remarkable that the incubation phenomenon of drug seeking was first discovered in laboratory rats and later also demonstrated to occur in smokers, 43 alcoholics, 44 and cocaine addicts 45 —such a direct translation to the human situation indicates high face, construct, and predictive validity of the incubation model of drug craving."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "construct validity",
      "value": null,

      "measures": "the degree to which the incubation of drug-seeking behavior in laboratory rats resembles the phenomenon in humans.",
      "compared": "incubation of drug-seeking in rats vs humans",
      "species": [

      ],
      "n": null,

      "verbatim": "It is remarkable that the incubation phenomenon of drug seeking was first discovered in laboratory rats and later also demonstrated to occur in smokers, 43 alcoholics, 44 and cocaine addicts 45 —such a direct translation to the human situation indicates high face, construct, and predictive validity of the incubation model of drug craving."
    },
    {

      "compared": "incubation of drug-seeking in rats vs humans",

    },
    {
      "statistic": "face validity",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the degree to which the alcohol-deprivation effect model for relapse in animals resembles relapse behavior seen in alcoholics.",
      "compared": "alcohol-deprivation effect model in animals vs relapse behavior in alcoholics",
      "species": [
        "animals",
        "alcoholics"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "In particular, the alcohol-deprivation-effect model provides excellent face validity to relapse behavior seen in alcoholics. 51"
    },
    {
      "statistic": "predictive power",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the extent to which medications that reduce relapse rates in alcoholics also reduce compulsive drinking during an alcohol deprivation effect in rats.",
      "compared": "medications reducing relapse rates in alcoholics vs medications reducing compulsive drinking in rats",
      "species": [
        "alcoholics",
        "rats"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "In alcoholics, medications that reduce relapse rates, such as naltrexone and acamprosate, also reduce compulsive drinking during an ADE, 58 , 59 demonstrating the predictive power of this animal model."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "translational value",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the potential for drugs that normalize circadian drinking activity during the alcohol deprivation effect in rats to be transferred to the clinical situation.",
      "compared": "drugs normalizing circadian drinking in rats vs clinical situation",
      "species": [
        "rats",
        "humans"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "Drugs such as agomelatine or melatonin, which normalize circadian drinking activity during the ADE, 28 could easily be transferred to the clinical situation."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "identical results",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the similarity of hyperglutamatergic activity in different brain sites during withdrawal between alcohol-dependent rats and alcohol-dependent humans, which diminishes when withdrawal symptomatology subsides.",
      "compared": "glutamate levels during withdrawal in rats vs humans",
      "species": [
        "rats",
        "humans"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "For example, glutamate spectroscopy in alcohol-dependent rats and alcohol-dependent humans has yielded identical results: during withdrawal, both rats and humans demonstrate hyperglutamatergic activity in different brain sites that diminishes when withdrawal symptomatology subsides. 73"
    },
    {
      "statistic": "correlation",
      "value": 0.9,
      "unit": "correlation",
      "measures": "the correlation between the number of responses on the inactive lever in mice and rats, suggesting a difference in lever pressing as a reinforcing activity.",
      "compared": "inactive lever responding in mice vs rats",
      "species": [
        "mice",
        "rats"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "Considering the number of responses on the inactive lever, mice and rats should be viewed differently, since in the former, lever pressing per se seems to be a reinforcing activity. 8 Thus, in a reinstatement test, mice may exhibit high inactive lever responding."
    },
